subject: ela
skillName: Tell a story or recount an experience
intro: When you tell a story or share an experience, the best descriptions include relevant, descriptive details. A detail is relevant when it helps the listener understand what happened, what you saw, or how it felt. A vague description tells the listener almost nothing. A detailed description paints a picture. The goal is to speak in complete sentences, clearly, and loudly enough to be heard, while choosing details that matter. Ask yourself: Would a listener who was not there understand exactly what I mean? If the answer is no, add a better detail.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a birthday party she attended.

Description A: 'It was a fun party. There were things to do and food to eat. I had a good time.'

Description B: 'At Maya's birthday party, we decorated cupcakes with pink frosting and sprinkles, and then played a relay race in the backyard. The cupcakes were sweet and I won the relay race by one step.'

Which description is better, and what makes it better?

steps: Description A is vague. 'Things to do' and 'food to eat' are not specific — every party has those.
Description B names the specific activities: decorating cupcakes and a relay race.
Description B includes sensory details: 'pink frosting and sprinkles,' 'sweet.'
Description B includes an exciting, specific outcome: winning the relay race by one step.
These details help a listener picture exactly what happened.
solution.answer: Description B is better. It uses specific, relevant details — the type of food (cupcakes with pink frosting), the activities (decorating and relay race), and the outcome (winning by one step). Description A is too vague to help a listener understand what the party was actually like.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a trip to the beach.

Description A: 'We went to the beach and did stuff. The water was cold. It was a long day.'

Description B: 'We drove two hours to Redondo Beach. The waves were so big they knocked my little brother over, and we both laughed until our stomachs hurt. We stayed until sunset and the sky turned orange and pink.'

What specific details in Description B make it more effective?

steps: Description B names the specific beach: Redondo Beach.
It describes the size of the waves and their effect: they knocked my brother over.
It includes a specific emotional moment: 'we laughed until our stomachs hurt.'
It has a time and visual detail: they stayed until sunset and describes the colors.
Each detail answers a question a listener might have: Where? What happened? How did it feel? When?
solution.answer: Description B is effective because it answers the listener's natural questions: Where did you go? What happened? How did it feel? What did it look like? Every detail is relevant to the experience and helps the listener picture the trip. Description A is too general to create any picture at all.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting the story of finding a lost dog.

Description A: 'I found a dog outside once. I helped it. The owner was happy.'

Description B: 'One afternoon I found a small tan dog sitting by our mailbox, shaking and without a collar. I gave it some water and stayed with it while my mom called the number on a sign down the street. An hour later, a girl named Lucia came running and hugged the dog for a whole minute.'

Identify at least three specific details in Description B that make it better than Description A.

steps: Detail 1: 'small tan dog' — describes the dog's size and color, making it real.
Detail 2: 'sitting by our mailbox, shaking and without a collar' — specific location and state of the dog.
Detail 3: 'gave it some water' — a specific action taken to help.
Detail 4: 'my mom called the number on a sign down the street' — explains exactly how they found the owner.
Detail 5: 'a girl named Lucia came running and hugged the dog for a whole minute' — a specific, vivid ending.
solution.answer: Description B is far better because of its specific details: the dog is described (small, tan, shaking, no collar); the location is named (by the mailbox); the actions are clear (giving water, calling the number on the sign); and the ending is vivid (Lucia hugging the dog for a full minute). Description A tells us nothing — any listener would walk away with no picture of what happened.

items.prompt:
A student is telling a story about cooking with a grandparent.

Description A: 'My grandma and I cooked something good. She showed me how to do it. It was delicious.'

Description B: 'My abuela and I made chicken tamales on a Sunday afternoon. She showed me how to spread the masa with the back of a spoon, and I kept making mine too thick. She laughed and fixed each one without saying a word. When they came out of the pot, the kitchen smelled like corn and chile, and mine tasted the best — at least that's what she told me.'

How do the details in Description B help the listener understand what this experience meant to the student?

steps: The description names what they made (chicken tamales) and when (Sunday afternoon).
It includes a specific action the student struggled with (spreading masa, making it too thick).
It shows the grandmother's character through action: she laughed and fixed each one without a word — patient and kind.
It includes a sensory detail: the kitchen smelled like corn and chile.
It ends with a warm, specific moment: the grandmother told her hers tasted best.
Together, these details show this was not just cooking — it was a loving, funny, memorable experience.
solution.answer: Description B's details show the listener not just what happened, but what it felt like. The specific struggle (masa too thick), the grandmother's quiet response (fixing each one without a word), the smell, and the final compliment all add up to a picture of a warm, funny, meaningful afternoon. Description A could describe any meal ever cooked — it tells us nothing about the experience.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a time she got lost at a store.

Description A: 'I got lost once. I was scared. Then I found my mom.'

Description B: 'I was looking at the toy aisle at the grocery store when I turned around and my mom was gone. My heart started beating fast and I stood still for a minute, not sure which way to go. I walked to the front of the store and told the lady at the register. She called my mom's name over the loudspeaker, and my mom came rushing around the corner holding a head of lettuce. I never ran into someone's arms so fast in my life.'

How do specific details help a listener feel what the experience was like for the student?

steps: The setting is specific: toy aisle at a grocery store.
The physical feeling is described: 'heart started beating fast' — this helps the listener feel the fear.
The student's actions are specific: stood still, walked to the front, told the cashier.
The loudspeaker announcement is a vivid, relatable detail.
The mom's small funny detail (holding lettuce) makes the reunion real and warm.
The final sentence — 'I never ran into someone's arms so fast' — sums up the emotional relief.
solution.answer: Description B is powerful because every detail puts the listener in the moment. The location, the physical feeling, the decision-making process, and the funny reunion detail (mom with the lettuce) all work together to re-create what it felt and looked like. Description A is three sentences that say almost nothing — a listener would feel nothing from it.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a school field trip to the fire station.

Description A: 'We went somewhere cool and learned things. There was big equipment. I liked it.'

Description B: 'Our class visited the Riverside Fire Station on Thursday. We saw a fire truck up close — the tires were taller than our teacher! A firefighter named Carlos put on his full gear in under one minute while we counted out loud. Afterward, we each got to spray water from a real hose.'

Which description uses more relevant details? Choose one specific detail from the better description and explain why it is effective.
items.hint: A relevant detail is one that helps a listener understand what happened, who was there, or what it felt like.

steps: Description B uses more relevant details.
It names the location (Riverside Fire Station) and the day (Thursday).
It includes a comparison that helps the listener visualize the size of the truck ('taller than our teacher').
It names a specific person (Carlos) and includes a timed action (under one minute).
It ends with a memorable activity: spraying a real fire hose.
Each detail answers a question: Where? What did you see? What happened? What did you do?
solution.answer: Description B uses more relevant details. One strong example is 'the tires were taller than our teacher' — this comparison makes the size of the fire truck easy to picture. Instead of saying 'the truck was big,' the student gives a detail that helps the listener actually see how big it was. Description A uses words like 'cool' and 'liked it' that mean almost nothing without specifics.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting a story about watching a thunderstorm.

Description A: 'There was a bad storm one night. It was loud and scary. We watched from inside.'

Description B: 'Last Tuesday night, a thunderstorm rolled in right after dinner. The lightning lit up the whole sky over the mountains, and thunder shook the windows three seconds later. My little sister pressed her face against the glass, and every time there was a flash she whispered, \"whoa.\"'

Identify two specific details from Description B. For each detail, explain what question it answers for the listener.
items.hint: Think about questions a listener might ask: When did it happen? What did it look, sound, or feel like? Who was there?

steps: Detail 1: 'Last Tuesday night, right after dinner' — this answers WHEN the story happened, placing the listener in a specific moment.
Detail 2: 'lightning lit up the whole sky over the mountains' — this answers WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE, helping the listener visualize the storm.
Detail 3 (bonus): 'thunder shook the windows three seconds later' — answers WHAT IT SOUNDED AND FELT LIKE.
Detail 4 (bonus): The sister whispering 'whoa' at each flash — adds a character and an emotional reaction.
Each detail either places us in the scene or helps us feel what it was like to be there.
solution.answer: Detail 1: 'Last Tuesday night, a thunderstorm rolled in right after dinner' — this answers WHEN. It places the listener at a specific time rather than just 'one night.' Detail 2: 'lightning lit up the whole sky over the mountains' — this answers WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE. A listener can picture a dramatic sky instead of just imagining a generic storm. Description A uses vague words ('bad,' 'loud,' 'scary') that every storm could earn — the details in B make this storm specific and real.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting the experience of performing in a school play.

Description A: 'I was in a play. I had a part. I was nervous but I did okay.'

Description B: 'In our class play about ocean animals, I played a sea turtle named Coral. My costume had a green cardboard shell that kept sliding to the side. When I said my big line — \"The ocean is my home and I will protect it!\" — my voice came out louder than I expected, and the audience clapped.'

How do the specific details in Description B make the experience feel real and meaningful to a listener?
items.hint: Think about details that name specific things, describe what happened physically, and tell how the student felt.

steps: The description names the play's topic (ocean animals) and the student's character (Coral, a sea turtle).
The costume detail (green cardboard shell sliding to the side) is funny and specific — listeners can picture it.
The big line is quoted exactly, letting the listener hear what the student said.
The surprise in the student's own voice ('louder than I expected') captures the feeling of the moment.
The audience clapping is a specific, satisfying ending.
Together, these details make this performance feel real, funny, and triumphant.
solution.answer: Description B makes the experience feel real because every part is specific: the play's topic, the student's character name, the sliding costume, the exact line, the surprise at her own voice, and the applause. A listener can see the green cardboard shell slipping, hear the line, and feel the relief and excitement of the clap. Description A says 'I did okay' — that is almost no information at all.

items.prompt:
A student is telling a story about getting a new pet fish.

Description A: 'We got a fish. I named it. I take care of it every day.'

Description B: 'My family got a betta fish last weekend, and I named him Captain Blue because his fins are the brightest blue I have ever seen. Every morning before school, I feed him five pellets and watch him dart to the surface to catch them. He always ignores the first two before he eats.'

The student in Description B uses specific, relevant details. Choose one detail you think is the most effective. Explain what it shows the listener that the vague description cannot.
items.hint: The best details show something specific about what happened, what the student observed, or what makes this experience personal.

steps: Option 1: 'Captain Blue because his fins are the brightest blue I have ever seen' — this names the fish and explains the name with evidence from observation.
Option 2: 'I feed him five pellets and watch him dart to the surface' — this shows a specific daily routine and an action.

Option 3: 'He always ignores the first two before he eats' — this is the best detail because it shows the student has paid close enough attention to notice a habit. This turns the fish into a real character with personality.
Description A says 'I take care of it every day' — this is a claim, not a detail.
The best details show, they don't just tell.
solution.answer: The most effective detail is: 'He always ignores the first two before he eats.' This is remarkable because it shows the student has watched the fish closely enough to notice a specific behavior. It turns Captain Blue from 'a pet fish' into a creature with a personality and habits. Description A only claims the student takes care of the fish; Description B proves it with an observation no one could make without paying real attention.

items.prompt:
A student is describing a time she helped a neighbor after a snowstorm.

Description A: 'After the snow, I helped an old lady near my house. She thanked me.'

Description B: 'After the big snowstorm on Saturday, I saw our neighbor Mrs. Flores trying to push her walker through three feet of snow to get to her mailbox. I grabbed the shovel from our porch and cleared a path from her door to the mailbox and back. It took about twenty minutes and my arms ached. She held both my hands when I was done and said, \"You are a good person.\"'

How do the details in Description B show the listener both what happened AND what kind of person the storyteller is?
items.hint: Look for details that show action, effort, and the moment at the end.

steps: The opening detail (Mrs. Flores with a walker in three feet of snow) shows why the student acted — it was urgent.
The student grabs the shovel without being asked — this shows initiative.
Clearing the path 'from her door to the mailbox and back' shows thoroughness.
Twenty minutes and aching arms shows real effort — not just a quick gesture.
Mrs. Flores holding both hands and saying 'You are a good person' is the emotional peak.
Together, these details show both what happened and the student's character: observant, caring, and hardworking.
solution.answer: Description B shows what happened AND who the storyteller is. The details reveal a person who noticed a neighbor struggling without being told (observant), grabbed a shovel without being asked (proactive), did the whole job (thorough), and stuck it out even when their arms ached (determined). The moment at the end — Mrs. Flores holding both hands and speaking those words — earns its weight because the listener witnessed all the effort that led to it. Description A says the same thing in eight words but tells the listener nothing about the person.
